prize_parts.citation: For the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: IceCube is a clue from nature in the sense I care about. A cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice was instrumented to answer a question that could not be settled by thought, and it returned an unexpected result: a diffuse flux of PeV-scale neutrinos of astrophysical origin, seen in 2013 and since confirmed in through-going muons, cascades and starting events. The later associations with TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane give that flux physical meaning, and the whole programme opens a genuinely new window on the origin of cosmic rays. The committee has rewarded this type of discovery before, where an instrument and a result are inseparable. Reading colleagues' openings, I find that the instrument-driven case is stronger than my own opening conveyed, since Pearce, Lindroth and Olsson all stress the same two points: the flux is established independently of any single source identification, and the detector concept is itself a major achievement. The credited trio is workable. Halzen is the driver of the AMANDA-to-IceCube path, Karle was central to design, construction and early analysis, and Spiering to the science and the collaboration.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. IceCube is a collaboration of hundreds, and the AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers lie outside the credited names, so three names will be read by some as arbitrary; Johansson even asks whether Karle should be replaced. A second reservation is that IceCube has the narrowest base of support among the front-runners, with only two first places, only two top-three rankings and a rank of 7 from Johansson, whereas topological insulators have six top-three rankings. If the committee prefers a field where the discoverers are unambiguous and the maturity is beyond question, B008 or B035 is the safer choice. Finally, the source-identification story is still statistically moderate, so one could argue the prize ought to wait for firmer point-source astronomy, although I regard the diffuse-flux discovery itself as sufficiently secure.

responses.point: IceCube is the instrument-driven discovery he weighs most heavily; the Nobel-level question is the detector concept and the discovery of the diffuse flux, not any single source, and a fair configuration needs a judgement on leadership versus technical founders.
responses.response: I agree on both counts, and your framing answers the maturity worry: the prize should cite the flux and the detector, not TXS 0506+056 or NGC 1068, which remain moderate in significance. On the allocation I would resist trimming to Halzen and Spiering alone, since Karle's role in the design, construction and first analysis of the detector is what turns the concept into the discovery. I do not think the prize can be made airtight with respect to AMANDA, and I would prefer that we say so openly instead of pretending the trio is the unique solution.

responses.point: IceCube is an impressive experiment and the flux is firmly established, but credit within a large collaboration is hard to draw, and she places it only seventh, relying on colleagues for the astroparticle judgement; she also asks whether Karle should replace one of the other two names and ranks circuit QED first.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously and I do not have a decisive argument for Karle over Spiering that is independent of the collaboration's own history. Where I part company is on weight: circuit QED is a fine achievement, but it follows the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and you yourself note that the committee may want a gap. IceCube has no such neighbouring recognition, and a collaboration problem is not a reason to pass over the opening of a new astronomical window; we solved a similar problem for gravitational waves.

responses.point: Topological insulators are a new quantum state of matter, predicted and then seen in HgTe, with the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio forming a clean configuration; he ranks it first and sees recognition as timely or overdue.
responses.response: I agree that B008 is a strong candidate, which is why it is my first alternative, and I ranked it second in my own opening. My qualification is that the trio is not as clean as you suggest: Johansson and Mehlig both note that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe system that Molenkamp then measured, so the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp configuration will be contested. Zhang's death also removes the one person whose omission would be most awkward, which may soften the issue, but I would want the citation to be written carefully around the quantum spin Hall effect and not the whole of topological matter.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are her first choice: mature, confirmed worldwide at the 1e-18 level, with Katori and Ye as a compact pair, and she regards circuit QED as timely but possibly dampened by the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I accept that B035 is mature and cleanly attributed, and I find the relativistic-geodesy and fundamental-constants applications persuasive, so it deserves serious consideration. My hesitation is only that its significance is chiefly one of precision, whereas IceCube found something nature had not told us before. I would not oppose a clock prize if the committee finds the IceCube credit too diffuse, and I would note that the pending redefinition of the second makes the timing attractive.

uncertainties: Whether Karle or another founder should be credited alongside Halzen and Spiering, and how to treat the AMANDA and DUMAND precursors.
Whether the committee will view the detector or the diffuse-flux discovery as the cited achievement, and whether expert reports can settle that.
How robust the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 associations will prove, and whether independent confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD strengthens the case.
Whether the 2025 circuit prize and the 2016 topological-phase prize reduce the committee's appetite for B004 or B008.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the shortlisted candidates is a supervisor, close collaborator or Uppsala colleague. I note only that, as Secretary, I commission outside reports and that my training in theory makes me depend on experts for the detector and condensed-matter claims.
